title-group.article-title: Accuracy of AFM cantilever thermal calibration in fluid of varying viscosities

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Thermal calibration of atomic force microscopy (AFM) cantilever spring constant, k, is routinely performed by fitting the thermal displacement power spectral density (PSD) to a simple harmonic oscillator (SHO) model. Experiments performed in liquid present the choice of whether to also calibrate in liquid or to pre-calibrate in air, where reduced hydrodynamic drag produces a sharper resonance peak. It remains an open question whether this yields a more accurate calibration. Here we use a hydrodynamic model introduced by Sader and later extended by Bellon to generate thermal PSDs for two cantilevers of differing known stiffness across four media of increasing viscosity. We then fit each generated PSD with the SHO model used in experimental calibration (under various parameters and conditions). Iteratively fitting in the vicinity of the resonance peak, with logarithmic weighting and a fitted noise term, recovers the known spring constant to within 3% in every medium including the most viscous, where the fundamental mode of the softer cantilever is overdamped. We use this analysis to identify an optimal fitting strategy—in terms of window size, window center, and weighting—for experimentally reasonable cantilever properties and describe a general procedure for determining these parameters for other cantilevers. We show that the optimal fit-window width is not universal but can be determined for any cantilever and medium by applying the same analysis with different parameters. To confirm these results, we experimentally calibrated the same two types of cantilevers in air and liquid and obtained k values that agreed closely, despite several-fold changes in resonance frequency and quality factor upon immersion. These results demonstrate that AFM cantilevers intended for liquid-phase measurements can be reliably calibrated in situ, without recourse to a separate calibration in air.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Atomic force microscopy (AFM) is a powerful tool for applying and measuring mechanical forces at the single-molecule level, enabling direct probing of biomolecular mechanics. AFM-based single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) has been applied across a wide range of biological systems, including protein folding, [1–3] ligand-receptor binding, [4, 5] DNA and polymer elasticity, [6, 7] lipid bilayer mechanics, [8] and cell adhesion and mechanotransduction [9]. To retain biological relevance, AFM measurements of these systems must be performed in aqueous buffer.

In an SMFS experiment, the tip of a cantilever is brought into contact with a sample (e.g. a single protein molecule tethered to a surface or embedded in a lipid bilayer) and then retracted while the cantilever deflection is measured (figure 1(a)). The cantilever behaves as a linear spring obeying Hooke’s law, F = kx, where k is the cantilever spring constant and x is the cantilever deflection. The deflection is measured using the optical lever method, where the displacement of a laser beam reflected from the cantilever onto a photodetector is recorded as a voltage signal and converted to deflection through calibration of the inverse optical lever sensitivity (invOLS) (figure 1(b)) [10, 11]. InvOLS is most directly calibrated by pressing the cantilever tip against a rigid surface, where the photodetector voltage tracks the known piezo displacement and the invOLS is obtained as the inverse of the slope of the deflection signal versus piezo displacement. This invOLS depends on the index of refraction of the medium, the cantilever geometry, the optical setup, the laser power, and other factors. Therefore, invOLS must be redetermined whenever the cantilever is reloaded into the instrument or whenever any aspect of the optical alignment is changed; invOLS values for the same cantilever in air and liquid can differ substantially. Equally important to the invOLS calibration is the calibration of k, which is the focus of this work (figure 1(c)). Uncertainties in the spring constant directly propagate into all derived quantities, including measured forces, contour lengths, energy landscapes, and kinetic parameters extracted from single-molecule experiments [12]. Accurate calibration of k has therefore long been recognized as a central requirement for quantitative AFM force measurements, motivating the development of reference calibration methods, traceable force standards, and formal uncertainty analyses [13, 14].

caption.p: (a) Schematic of an AFM-based single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) assay of a membrane protein. A cantilever tip is brought into contact with a membrane protein in a lipid bilayer and retracted while deflection is monitored via the optical lever method. A laser beam reflected from the back of the cantilever onto a position-sensitive photodiode records the deflection signal, from which the applied force is recovered via calibrated inverse optical lever sensitivity (invOLS) and spring constant (k). (b) Schematic of invOLS calibration. The cantilever tip is pressed against a hard surface and the deflection signal is recorded as a function of piezo displacement. The inverse of the slope of this curve gives the invOLS. (c) Schematic of k calibration via the thermal noise method. With the cantilever freely suspended above the surface, thermal fluctuations drive random motion. The equipartition theorem relates the variance of this motion to k. In practice, the amplitude is recorded and analyzed in the frequency domain to extract k.

sec.p: The mechanical response of an AFM cantilever is conventionally modeled as a damped harmonic oscillator characterized by three parameters: the spring constant k, the resonance frequency f0, and the quality factor Q [15, 16]. The thermal motion of the cantilever can be characterized in the frequency domain through its power spectral density (PSD), which describes how the cantilever’s thermal displacement energy is distributed across frequencies (figure 2). For an underdamped oscillator (Q > ½), the PSD is sharply peaked at f0, with a flat white-noise plateau at f < f0 and f−4 decay at f > f0 (figure 2(a)). As damping increases and Q decreases toward and below the critical damping condition (Q = ½), this peak progressively broadens and weakens, disappearing entirely once the oscillator is overdamped, although the total area under the PSD remains constant to satisfy the equipartition theorem. The PSDs in figure 2 assume that the damping experienced by the cantilever is frequency-independent. In actual experiments, a cantilever immersed in a viscous fluid experiences hydrodynamic loading that varies with oscillation frequency, which modifies the shape of the thermal PSD in ways that the damped harmonic oscillator model cannot fully capture.

caption.p: Analytical power spectral density (PSD) of a single-mode damped harmonic oscillator (equation (2)), illustrating how quality factor (Q), spring constant (k), and resonance frequency (f0) each shape the thermal noise spectrum under the idealized assumption of frequency-independent damping. (a) PSD for an underdamped oscillator in air (Q = 5.0, blue) and an overdamped oscillator in liquid (Q = 0.4, orange), with f0 and k held fixed. The air spectrum exhibits a sharp, well-resolved resonance peak, while the liquid spectrum is broad and shallow, with most of its spectral weight shifted to frequencies below f0. (b) PSD curves illustrating the independent effects of increasing k (blue to green, same f0) and increasing f0 (blue to orange, same k) at fixed Q. Increasing k lowers the low-frequency plateau without shifting the peak position, whereas increasing f0 shifts the entire resonance to higher frequency while lowering the plateau height.

sec.p: Here Sw is an additional term that can be added to model frequency-independent white-noise background deriving from detection noise or other contributions uncorrelated with the cantilever’s thermal motion.

Because it involves three fit parameters—or four including Sw—there is a concern that fitting equation (2) will not yield an accurate thermal calibration if the experimental PSD does not contain enough information to constrain all parameters. This is a special concern in liquid, where damping suppresses the resonance peak (figure 2(a)). Conversely, invOLS calibration in liquid can be more facile, especially for soft cantilevers, because aqueous solution screens electrostatic interactions between the cantilever and surface. This allows the tip to be brought in contact with the surface without the snap-to-contact and adhesion artifacts that can make it difficult to accurately measure the surface-contact slope in air (figure S1). There are also practical advantages to calibrating a cantilever immediately before it is used or even from thermal fluctuations recorded during the single-molecule assay itself.

These considerations raise a fundamental question: should cantilevers intended for liquid experiments be calibrated in air beforehand or calibrated in situ within the aqueous measurement environment? This choice is unique to AFM. While thermal PSD fitting is also used to calibrate optical traps and magnetic tweezers, [24] those traps cannot be moved between media in the way a cantilever can. It is possible to address this question using theory to predict the PSDs of cantilevers with known parameters, which can then be fit with equation (2). Such an approach, however, requires an accurate physical model of cantilever thermal oscillations in liquid.

A physically complete description of the cantilever’s thermal motion must account for its frequency-dependent drag arising from its complex hydrodynamic function. Such a description was developed by Sader [22] and later elaborated by Bellon [25]. For a cantilever idealized as a thin, long rectangular beam immersed in a viscous fluid, Sader showed that the hydrodynamic loading exerted by the surrounding fluid is captured by a dimensionless hydrodynamic function Γ(ω), whose real part accounts for the added mass of fluid entrained by the moving beam and whose imaginary part accounts for the viscous drag it experiences [22]. Because Γ(ω) varies with frequency, the effective mass and damping of the cantilever are frequency-dependent, in contrast to the assumption underlying equation (2). Building on this framework, Bellon applied the fluctuation-dissipation theorem to each flexural mode of the cantilever to derive the thermal displacement PSD of a real beam of specified geometry in a fluid of specified density and viscosity [25]. The resulting PSD departs qualitatively from the Lorentzian form of equation (2) in lacking a flat low-frequency plateau and exhibiting a more-gradual high-frequency rolloff.

Here we compare the accuracy of thermal calibration of k in air and liquid conditions—and in different viscosities—by using the Sader-Bellon model to predict PSDs of cantilevers with known parameters; we then fit these PSDs with the Lorentzian equation used in experimental fitting (equation (2)). We are not aware of prior studies employing this approach, which have mostly compared different experimental calibration methods [19, 23, 26, 27] or calibration under different experimental conditions [28, 29]. Less systematic attention has been given to the bias introduced by the mathematical model used to fit the thermal spectrum, particularly under strongly damped liquid conditions. An advantage of our approach is that the underlying value of k in the generated PSDs is known a priori and thus can be used as a basis for calculating bias in the fit results, whereas the stiffness of real cantilevers can vary significantly from the manufacturer’s nominal value. We were thus able to optimize the fitting in terms of width, weighting, and number of iterations to minimize the bias. We tested these optimized conditions, as well as our conclusion that cantilevers can be accurately calibrated in liquid, through test experiments on two types of cantilevers relevant to SMFS. Although we focus on SMFS, the results are relevant to any AFM measurement that requires calibrated force in liquid, such as nanoindentation of cells and soft materials, colloidal-probe force measurements, and mechanobiology [30–32].

sec.title: Sader-Bellon viscous PSD model
sec.p: PSDs were generated for four fluid media spanning more than three orders of magnitude in dynamic viscosity: air (ρ = 1.18 kg m−3, η = 1.84 ×10−5 Pa·s), water (ρ = 997.05 kg m−3, η = 8.90 ×10−4 Pa·s), 4 M NaH2PO4 (ρ = 1313.00 kg m−3, η = 7.40 ×10−3 Pa·s), and 75% glycerol (ρ = 1191.95 kg m−3, η = 3.20 ×10−2 Pa·s) [28, 33, 34]. Our implementation of the Sader-Bellon model in Python is freely available, (see Data availability statement below).

sec.title: Cantilever parameters
sec.p: We modeled two silicon-nitride cantilevers relevant to SMFS experiments: a shorter, stiffer, and higher-frequency cantilever (BL-AC40TS; k = 90.0 pN nm−1, L = 38 µm, b = 16 µm, h = 0.2 µm, ρ = 3170 kg m−3) and a longer, softer, and lower-frequency cantilever (MLCT-Bio B; k = 20.0 pN nm−1, L = 210 µm, b = 20 µm, h = 0.55 µm, ρ = 3170 kg m−3). These geometries and material properties were used to compute the cantilever mass mc and, together with each medium’s density, the entrained fluid mass mf. These cantilever types were also used in the experimental calibration measurements described below, admitting comparison.

sec.title: Resonance frequency estimation
SHO fitting procedure
sec.p: Several related approaches were used to fit the calculated PSDs with the SHO Lorentzian model of equation (2). Minimization was performed with differential evolution (scipy.optimize.differential_evolution), rather than a gradient-based method, to avoid sensitivity to the initial parameter guesses. In all fits, the model PSD was sampled on a uniform frequency grid with 38.15 Hz spacing, matching the frequency resolution of the experimental spectra. Fits were performed under four conditions, differing in whether the spectrum carried a detection-noise floor and in how the residuals were weighted. Residuals were computed either on linear PSD values, so the sum of the squared residuals is dominated by the high-amplitude points near the resonance peak, or on the logarithm of the PSD, which weights all sampled frequencies comparably. For the noiseless spectra, Sw was fixed at zero and the three remaining parameters (f0, Q, k) were fitted under both linear and logarithmic weighting. Spectra carrying noise were generated by adding a frequency-independent background of Sw = 2 ×10−26 m2 Hz−1 to the Sader-Bellon PSD, chosen to approximate the detection-noise level of the experimental thermal spectra, and were fitted with Sw as a fourth free parameter, under both weightings. Fits to experimental thermal spectra, which inherently contain a detection-noise floor, were always fitted with Sw as a free parameter.

sec.title: Bias computation
Experimental calibration
sec.p: Experimental thermal calibration was performed on BL-AC40TS and MLCT-Bio B cantilevers using an Asylum Research (Oxford Instruments) Cypher ES AFM at 25 °C. For each cantilever, invOLS and thermal k were first calibrated in air using the instrument’s air holder. The cantilever was then transferred to a perfusion holder and the invOLS redetermined in Tris-buffered saline (20 mM Tris, 150 mM NaCl) before calibration in that medium. The invOLS was determined from force curves acquired against a freshly cleaved mica surface, with the trigger set to 1 V of deflection in both air and buffer. The slope was taken from a linear fit to the contact region of the retract curve, where the tip is in hard contact with the surface (figure 1(b)). In each medium, five replicate calibrations were performed. Each replicate consisted of a new invOLS determination followed by acquisition of a thermal spectrum, and each spectrum was converted to displacement units using its own paired invOLS value (a one-to-one pairing). For each calibration, the thermal PSD was computed from consecutive 26.2 ms deflection time records, each Fourier-transformed to give a spectrum with 38.15 Hz frequency resolution. Approximately 250 such spectra were averaged to reduce the statistical scatter of the PSD. The spectra extended from 38.15 Hz to 8 MHz, except for the MLCT-Bio B in air, which extended to 2 MHz. Data were fit to the SHO model with Sw term (equation (2)) and logarithmic weighting using the local strategy with αα = 2.5. Fitting was performed using the same custom Python routines applied to the theoretical data to allow direct comparison.

The replicate variance of k was separated into contributions from thermal PSD fitting and invOLS variability. The statistical uncertainty of each fitted k was estimated from the parameter covariance matrix of the final log-weighted fit. These variances were averaged and the remaining replicate variance, attributed to variability in determining invOLS, was obtained by subtracting the fitting variance from the total variance of k, so that the two contributions combine in quadrature to give the standard deviation reported in table 3.

sec.title: A physically realistic PSD, fit with the experimentally relevant SHO model
sec.p: To probe how the choice of fitting strategy affects calibration accuracy, we generated thermal displacement PSDs using the Sader-Bellon model, which captures the frequency-dependent hydrodynamic loading experienced by a cantilever oscillating in a viscous fluid. Unlike the SHO approximation, the resulting PSD lacks a flat, white-noise plateau at low frequency and falls off more gradually than f−4 at high frequency. Despite this, we fit each model PSD with the same SHO Lorentzian model that experimentalists routinely use to calibrate real cantilevers, regardless of the medium (equation (2)). Sader showed that in the limit of small dissipation and in the vicinity of a resonance peak, the frequency response of a cantilever in fluid reduces analytically to that of a SHO, with f0 and Q given by equations 33 and 35 of Reference 22. Thus, at least for sufficiently weak damping and for a sufficiently narrow frequency range around f0, equation (2) is expected to adequately describe the shape of the hydrodynamically realistic PSD. One question remains how rapidly it ceases to be adequate as damping increases, as in liquid.

This strategy was applied to two cantilevers relevant to SMFS experiments: a stiff, shorter cantilever (BL-AC40TS) [35] and a soft, longer cantilever (MLCT-Bio B), [36] each modeled in four media: air, water, 4 M NaH2PO4, and 75% glycerol. The latter two media were chosen to admit comparison with the study of Pirzer and Hugel [28]. For each cantilever-medium combination, equation (2) was fit using two strategies: a local fit restricted to a window around the resonance peak and a global fit spanning the full measured spectrum. The local fit was performed iteratively, recentering the fit window on the newly recovered resonance frequency until convergence. The consequences of fitting only once, without this recentering, were also examined separately.

sec.title: Local fitting near the resonance peak accurately recovers the spring constant across all media

caption.p: Local and global SHO fit parameters for the modeled BL-AC40TS and MLCT-Bio B cantilevers across four media of increasing viscosity, obtained with residuals computed on linear PSD values. The local fit was performed iteratively with α = 3.5 while the global fit spanned the full spectrum.

fn.p: δk denotes the percentage bias of the fitted k relative to the input k (equation (6)).

sec.p: These fits used residuals computed on linear PSD values. Repeating them with residuals computed on the logarithm of the PSD degrades the recovered k substantially, and progressively so with damping. The local-fit bias goes from +6.6% in air to −25.9% in 75% glycerol for BL-AC40TS, and from +4.9% to −36.8% for MLCT-Bio B (table S1). Logarithmic weighting distributes the fit across all sampled frequencies, drawing it toward the off-resonance regions where the Sader-Bellon and SHO lineshapes diverge, which is precisely what the local window is intended to exclude.

sec.title: Global fitting degrades as viscosity increases
sec.p: In contrast to the local fit, fitting the SHO Lorentzian with linear weighting over a global range spanning the full measured spectrum produced low bias only in air, with progressively larger bias once the cantilever was immersed in liquid. For the BL-AC40TS cantilever, the linear global fit k bias was +2.4% in air, +5.8% in water, +11.5% in 4 M NaH2PO4, and +13.5% in 75% glycerol, while for the MLCT-Bio B cantilever, the bias was +2.3% in air, and +9.9%, +13.7%, and +14.1% across the same media (table 1). The air panel of figure 3 shows the global fit can be accurate in k while being visibly misaligned with much of the spectrum. The fitted curve overestimates the low-frequency plateau by two orders of magnitude, but those points contribute negligibly to a linear residual sum, so the recovered k is set almost entirely by the peak. As viscosity increases, the mismatched regions move closer to the peak in amplitude and can no longer be ignored.

Under logarithmic weighting, the global fit fails outright, returning Q below 1 in every medium and k overestimated by up to a factor of ∼13 (table S1). With all frequencies weighted comparably, the fit is forced to accommodate the low-frequency plateau and the shallow high-frequency rolloff that the SHO form cannot reproduce.

sec.title: Iterative fitting is needed in more-viscous media
sec.p: The local fits presented in figure 3 were performed iteratively. The fit window was recentered on the newly recovered f0 after each fit, for a total of five iterations, to correct for cases in which the apparent peak of the PSD differs from the fluid-loaded f0. This recentering proves unnecessary in some conditions but essential in others. When the local fit is performed only once, with the window centered on the raw PSD peak, the recovered k for the stiff cantilever (BL-AC40TS) remains accurate in air (+2.4%) and water (+2.2%), with the departure from the iterative result growing in 4 M NaH2PO4 (+4.7%) and becoming large in 75% glycerol (+10.5%) (figure 4). The soft cantilever (MLCT-Bio B) exhibited the same breakdown but more severely, with non-iterative bias reaching +10.0% in 4 M NaH2PO4 and +21.3% in 75% glycerol (figure S3). This is consistent with its lower Q and corresponding larger separation between the apparent peak and the actual resonance, leading the window to be centered on a frequency well below f0. Iterative recentering was therefore adopted as the standard local fitting procedure throughout this work.

caption.p: Modeled thermal noise PSD of the BL-AC40TS cantilever (blue) with a non-iterative local SHO fit (red; window half-width α = 3.5), shown for (a) air, (b) water, (c) 4 M NaH2PO4, and (d) 75% glycerol. The dotted gray line marks fpeak, the apparent maximum of the PSD used to center the fit window, and the dashed gray line marks f0 calculated as discussed in section 2.3.

sec.title: An intermediate fit window width minimizes local fit bias

caption.p: Absolute bias in the iterative local-fit spring constant, |δk|, as a function of the fit window half-width α, for the BL-AC40TS cantilever in air, water, 4 M NaH2PO4, and 75% glycerol, using the noiseless Sader–Bellon PSD. The fit window spans [fpeak/α, fpeak × α] around the iteratively recentered peak. The bias is minimized near α = 3.5 (dashed vertical line), where it remains below 3% (gray shaded band) in all four media.

sec.p: This non-monotonic dependence reflects two competing failure modes of the local fit. At small α, the window is too narrow to resolve the width and shape of the resonance peak, particularly once that peak is broad and asymmetric under strong damping. The fit becomes underdetermined and increasingly biased. At large α, the window extends into the off-resonance wings, where the Sader-Bellon PSD departs most strongly from the SHO expectation. An intermediate α balances these two effects across all media.

The same sweep performed for the MLCT-Bio B cantilever showed the same U-shaped dependence, but with minima displaced to somewhat larger α (figure S4). At α = 3.5, the bias remains within 3% in all media for the soft cantilever as well, so the same window width serves both cantilevers. This illustrates a more general point that the optimal window width is not universal but depends on the cantilever and the medium, through the sharpness of the resonance. For experimental work in a particular cantilever-medium combination, the window width can be optimized directly by repeating the sweep presented here with the relevant cantilever dimensions and fluid properties using our freely available analysis code accompanying this work (see Data availability statement below).

sec.title: Fitting spectra with a noise floor requires logarithmic weighting
sec.p: The analysis above used noiseless spectra, representing only the thermal motion of the cantilever; experimental spectra sit on a detection-noise floor that can be modeled using the Sw term in equation (2) and that could alter the fitting strategy. To determine how the floor affects the choice of weighting, Sader-Bellon PSDs were regenerated with a white-noise floor of Sw = 2 ×10−26 m2 Hz−1 and fitted with the extended SHO model of equation (2) (i.e. including Sw as a fit parameter), using both linear and logarithmic residuals under otherwise identical conditions.

With the noise floor present, the two weightings diverge sharply for the local fit (table 2). Under linear weighting, the recovered k is biased by up to 13% in the viscous media for both cantilevers and the fitted noise floor is overestimated by roughly an order of magnitude for the BL-AC40TS cantilever and by 2–3 orders of magnitude for the MLCT-Bio B cantilever. For the MLCT-Bio B in air, the linear fit does not constrain Sw at all. Logarithmic weighting recovers k to within about 3% in every medium and, while it does not always accurately recover Sw, it constrains it well enough that k remains accurate (table 2; fits shown in figures S5 and S6). Full results for all four fit parameters are given in table S3. These biases were insensitive to the cantilever parameters assumed in the model. Concerted variation of the cantilever mass, thickness, width, and hydrodynamic loading in ways expected not to change k affected its recovered value by at most 0.3 percentage points (supplementary note 1). The biases are also insensitive to contamination from higher-order flexural modes, which lie well above the local fit window in any medium. Removing the second mode, which was included in all PSDs in this work, changed the recovered k by no more than 0.2 percentage points. Global fitting of the entire PSD gives poor results with both weightings (table S2). Thus, when fitting noise-containing data—including experimental data—we used the iterative local fit with logarithmic weighting.

caption.p: Local fits of the SHO model with Sw as a fit parameter using linear and logarithmic residual weighting, applied to Sader-Bellon PSDs with 2 × 10−26 m2 Hz−1 added white noise. All fits were iterative with α = 2.5.

sec.p: We argue that logarithmic weighting is more effective for the noise-containing data because the white-noise floor lies far below the resonance peak in the off-resonance region of the spectrum (figures S5 and S6). A fit with linear weighting is dominated by the high-amplitude points near the peak, leaving Sw effectively unconstrained. Failure to constrain one fit parameter can bias the other parameters, including k. Logarithmic weighting gives the off-resonance points comparable influence, better constraining the noise floor. This is the opposite of the noiseless case, where the off-resonance region is where the functional forms of the SHO and Sader-Bellon models diverge.

sec.title: Detection noise reshapes the window tradeoff
sec.p: The presence of a white-noise floor could in principle shift the optimal α for local fitting. To test this, we repeated the fit-window sweep of figure 5, now fitting to Sader-Bellon PSDs with 2 ×10−26 m2 Hz−1 added frequency-independent noise using equation (2) with logarithmic weighting and Sw as a fourth fit parameter.

For the BL-AC40TS cantilever, the noise floor reshaped the individual |δk| vs αα curves; now α = 2.5 provided sub-3% bias across media (figure 6). As in figure 5, the bias for all media except air was large at small αα because of poor sampling of the resonance peak. As α was increased, the bias initially decreased, passing through a minimum, then increased again in the more viscous media because the flat noise floor—rather than the mismatched Sader-Bellon wings—now dominated the off-resonance region. The same sweep for the MLCT-Bio B cantilever shows that α = 2.5 is likewise a good value (figure S7).

caption.p: Robustness of the fit-window choice to detection noise. The α sweep in figure 5 was repeated for the BL-AC40TS cantilever after adding a white-noise floor (Sw = 2 × 10−26 m2 Hz−1) to the Sader-Bellon PSD, representative of the detection-noise level of a typical AFM. Each spectrum was now fit with the noise-containing SHO model (equation (2)), with f0, Q, k, and Sw as fit parameters and logarithmic weighting.

sec.title: In situ calibration in buffer agrees with calibration in air
sec.p: Having used theoretical spectra to optimize a calibration strategy based on iterative local (αα = 2.5) fitting of the four-parameter SHO model (equation (2), including noise term) with logarithmic weighting, we sought to test this approach by fitting experimental thermal spectra of the two cantilevers measured in air and buffer (20 mM Tris HCl, 150 mM NaCl). Immersion in buffer strongly alters the thermal PSD of both cantilevers (figure 7). For the BL-AC40TS, f0 shifts from 93.8 kHz in air to 28.0 kHz in buffer and Q falls from 37.6 to 1.6 (table 3). The softer MLCT-Bio B is affected more severely, its f0 dropping from 13.8 kHz to 3.2 kHz and Q from 8.1 to 0.6, close to the critical damping condition (table 3). These shifts are the expected consequences of fluid loading, with entrained mass lowering f0 and viscous drag reducing Q.

caption.p: Experimental application of the optimized fitting strategy to two types of cantilevers. Experimental thermal noise PSDs (black) of freely oscillating cantilevers above a mica substrate were fit (orange) with the four-parameter SHO model (equation (2), including Sw term) using α = 2.5 and logarithmic weighting. Shown are representative results for the stiffer BL-AC40TS cantilever in (a) air and (b) buffer and for the softer MLCT-Bio B cantilever in (c) air and (d) buffer.

Experimental thermal calibration of the BL-AC40TS and MLCT-Bio B cantilevers in air and buffer. Spectra were analyzed with the four-parameter SHO model (equation (2), including Sw term) using αα = 2.5 and logarithmic weighting. Each entry is the mean ± standard deviation of five replicate measurements of the same cantilever; each thermal spectrum was paired with its own independent invOLS determination.

fn.p: The estimated uncertainties from thermal PSD fitting and invOLS variability, respectively, were: BL-AC40TS air, 0.4 and 3.5 pN nm−1; BL-AC40TS buffer, 0.3 and 1.0 pN nm−1; MLCT-Bio B air, 0.1 and 0.4 pN nm−1; MLCT-Bio B buffer, 0.7 and 0.6 pN nm−1.

sec.p: Despite pronounced changes in f0 and Q, the recovered k values were nearly unchanged between the two media, consistent with the understanding of k as a medium-independent material property of the cantilever. As seen in table 3, we measured k values for the stiffer BL-AC40TS cantilever in buffer that agreed within 1% of its value in air and for the softer MLCT-Bio B that agreed within 3%. Both are consistent with the few-percent differential bias predicted by our modeled analysis (table 2). The small residual differences are compatible with the additional experimental uncertainty in invOLS calibration, which must be redetermined in each medium and can be particularly challenging in air because of unscreened electrostatic interactions between the probe and the substrate, as illustrated in figure S1.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: We have used a physically realistic hydrodynamic model of cantilever thermal motion to test how the choice of fitting strategy affects thermal calibration of the spring constant across fluid viscosities spanning more than three orders of magnitude for two cantilever types directly relevant to SMFS experiments. We determined that, in the presence of white noise typical of experimental data, the best calibrations could be obtained by fitting a four-parameter SHO model (equation (2), including noise term Sw) in an iterative manner in the local vicinity of the first resonant peak (half-width α = 2.5, the optimum in the presence of noise) using logarithmic weighting. Application of this model to theoretical PSDs yielded k biases of <3% in water for both cantilever types; application of the model to experimental data showed agreement between air and buffer calibrations at the level of 1% for the stiffer cantilever and 3% for the softer cantilever. Taken together, these results indicate that AFM cantilevers intended for liquid-phase single-molecule measurements can be calibrated reliably in situ without the need for a separate calibration in air if appropriate fitting conditions are used. For cantilevers with substantially different properties from those investigated here, this conclusion can be checked and the fitting strategy perhaps refined by repeating our analysis with new parameter values using the same simulation code we have made freely available.
